title: Write Tag-Scoped GCP Firewall Rules in Terraform
intro: Two GCP incidents came from firewall rules: one targeted the wrong network tag (gcp-incident-001), and one got deleted by a cleanup (gcp-incident-004). Write both rules as code, scoped tightly, so they're reviewed and can't silently drift.

steps.prompt:
Write two google_compute_firewall resources on network "prod-vpc":
1. "allow_https_web": direction "INGRESS", an allow block with protocol "tcp" and ports ["443"], source_ranges ["0.0.0.0/0"], target_tags ["web"].
2. "allow_iap_ssh": direction "INGRESS", an allow block with protocol "tcp" and ports ["22"], source_ranges ["35.235.240.0/20"] (the IAP range only), and a description "SSH via IAP only - do not delete".
Each needs a name attribute: "allow-https-web" and "allow-iap-ssh".
steps.hint: resource "google_compute_firewall" "allow_https_web" { name = "allow-https-web" network = "prod-vpc" direction = "INGRESS" allow { protocol = "tcp" ports = ["443"] } source_ranges = ["0.0.0.0/0"] target_tags = ["web"] }. The allow block is nested; ports is a list of strings.
steps.fake_output:
Success! The configuration is valid.

Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
steps.explanation: HTTPS reaches only VMs tagged 'web'; SSH reaches VMs only from Google's IAP proxy range.
steps.why: In GCP, the target_tags line is the whole scope of a rule: leave it out and the rule applies to every VM in the network. Writing rules in Terraform means a wrong tag shows up in code review, and a cleanup that deletes the IAP rule by hand shows up as drift on the next plan. For stronger scoping, use target_service_accounts instead of tags, since tags can be added by anyone who can edit a VM (gcp-tutorial-005).
